chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) about the flint, the cane, and the wood — can one slaughter with them when a knife cannot be found? He said: When it tears the jugular veins, there is no problem with that.

key_terms.الأوداج: The jugular veins (awdaj, plural); the specific blood vessels whose severance validates Islamic slaughter
key_terms.العود: Wood/stick with a sharp edge or point; another permitted alternative instrument
key_terms.القصبة: Cane/reed with a sharp edge; another permitted alternative instrument
key_terms.المروة: Flint/sharp stone used for cutting; in early Islamic jurisprudence, one of the permitted substitutes for a knife in emergency slaughter
key_terms.فرى: To tear/cut cleanly; the technical term for the required severing action in ritual slaughter

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to slaughter an animal with flint, cane, or wood in Islam if no knife is available?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses a practical jurisprudential question about emergency slaughter. The companion Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj asked Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) whether it is permissible to slaughter an animal using sharp stones (flint), cane, or wood in the absence of a knife. The Imam's reply establishes that the determining criterion is not the instrument used, but whether the jugular veins are properly severed — if this condition is met, the slaughter is valid regardless of the tool employed.
